📋 Unsupervised Learning — Cheat Sheet

Everything from L1–L5 in one place. Clustering, density methods, and dimensionality reduction.

What Each Lesson Covers

LessonCore topicKey takeaway
L1: FundamentalsLearning without labelsFind structure in unlabelled data: clustering, dimensionality reduction, anomaly detection, generative modelling.
L2: K-MeansCentroid-based partitioning into k clustersMinimise inertia by alternating assign/update. Must scale; pick k with elbow + silhouette.
L3: HierarchicalNested clusters → dendrogramNo k upfront — cut the dendrogram where merge distances jump. Ward linkage is the default.
L4: DBSCANDensity-based clusters + noiseFinds arbitrary shapes and labels outliers (−1). No k needed; tune eps & min_samples.
L5: t-SNENon-linear 2D/3D visualisationPreserves local neighbourhoods for plotting. Distances/sizes between clusters aren't meaningful.

L1: Fundamentals

AspectDetail
DataUnlabelled — no target y. The algorithm finds structure on its own.
Main tasksClustering, dimensionality reduction, anomaly detection, generative modelling
EvaluationNo ground truth → use intrinsic metrics (silhouette, inertia) or downstream task performance, not accuracy
Helps supervised pipelinesFeature compression (PCA), cluster features, outlier removal before training
Note on generative modelsNot always unsupervised — they can be trained with labels too

L2: K-Means Clustering

Inertia = Σ ‖xᵢ − μ_cluster(i)‖²
silhouette s(i) = (b − a) / max(a, b)

a = mean distance to own cluster, b = mean distance to nearest other cluster. s near +1 = well clustered.

ConceptDetail
The KNumber of clusters — you choose it before fitting
AlgorithmAssign each point to nearest centroid → recompute centroids → repeat until stable
Must scale featuresUses Euclidean distance — large-scale features would dominate
InertiaTotal within-cluster squared distance — always decreases as k rises (so can't pick k alone)
Different results per runRandom centroid init → use n_init / k-means++ to stabilise
Elbow methodPlot inertia vs k, pick the elbow. Limitation: the elbow is often ambiguous → confirm with silhouette
⚠️ K-Means assumes roughly spherical, equally-sized clusters. It struggles with elongated or differently-sized shapes — clusters can look "mixed" in a 2D projection even when valid in full dimensions.

L3: Hierarchical Clustering

ConceptDetail
Agglomerative vs divisiveAgglomerative = bottom-up (merge); divisive = top-down (split). Agglomerative is the common one.
DendrogramTree of merges. A tall vertical line before a merge = those clusters are very dissimilar.
Choosing kCut the dendrogram horizontally where the vertical gaps are largest — count the lines you cross
Ward linkage (default)Merges the pair that minimises the increase in within-cluster variance — compact, balanced clusters
Single linkageDistance = closest pair. Prone to "chaining" — clusters string together through bridge points
scipylinkage() builds the linkage matrix (which clusters merged, at what distance, cluster size)
Advantage over K-MeansNo need to pick k upfront; the dendrogram reveals structure at every level

L4: DBSCAN

TermMeaning
Core pointHas ≥ min_samples neighbours within radius eps
Border pointWithin eps of a core point but not itself core
Noise (label −1)Neither core nor border — an outlier, explicitly flagged
epsNeighbourhood radius — pick from the "knee" of the k-nearest-neighbour distance plot
min_samplesDensity threshold — rule of thumb ≥ dimensions + 1 (often 2×dims)
StrengthLimitation
Finds arbitrary shapes; no k needed; isolates outliersStruggles when clusters have varying densities (one eps can't fit all)
Robust to outliers (unlike K-Means, which forces every point into a cluster)Sensitive to eps/min_samples; must scale features first

L5: t-SNE

ConceptDetail
PurposeNon-linear dimensionality reduction for visualising high-dimensional data in 2D/3D
perplexityRoughly "number of effective neighbours" (typical 5–50). Balances local vs global structure
Student t-distributionHeavy tails in the low-D space fix the crowding problem — gives distant points room so clusters don't collapse together
Non-deterministicRandom init → set random_state for reproducibility
PCA before t-SNEReduce to ~50 dims first → faster and denoises before the non-linear step
⚠️ Read t-SNE plots carefully. Only local neighbourhoods are meaningful. Cluster sizes, inter-cluster distances, and empty gaps are not interpretable. It's for visualisation, not for measuring or for feeding distances downstream.

Clustering Method Selector

SituationUse
Roughly spherical clusters, know k, large dataK-Means
Don't know k, want to see structure at all levelsHierarchical (dendrogram)
Arbitrary shapes, outliers present, unknown kDBSCAN
Just want to visualise high-dim clusterst-SNE (or PCA for a linear view)
Unsupervised Learning · L1

🌐 Fundamentals of Unsupervised Learning

Learning patterns from unlabelled data — clustering, dimensionality reduction, anomaly detection, and generative modelling.

What is Unsupervised Learning?

In supervised learning, every training example has a label — a correct answer the model learns to predict. You give it (X, y) pairs and it learns the mapping X → y.

In unsupervised learning there are no labels. You only have X. The model's job is to find hidden structure — patterns, groupings, compact representations — without being told what to look for.

The fundamental difference

Supervised: you tell the model what the answer looks like. It learns to predict it.

Unsupervised: all variables are treated symmetrically. There is no special "target" column. The model explores how all variables relate to each other and surfaces the structure it finds.

Key definitions

TermDefinition
ClusterA group of data points that are more similar to each other than to points outside the group
DimensionalityThe number of features (columns) in your dataset. High-dimensional data is hard to visualise or reason about directly
Latent structureHidden patterns in the data that are not directly observable but can be discovered by the model
Distribution P(X)The probability distribution that describes how likely each combination of feature values is in the data
RepresentationA transformed version of the data that is more compact, more informative, or easier to work with

Why do we need it?

  • Labels are expensive or unavailable — labelling millions of transactions requires expert time. Raw data is cheap; labels are not. Unsupervised learning extracts value from data you already have.
  • You don't know what you're looking for — you want to discover structure, not test a pre-formed hypothesis. The model reveals groupings you didn't know existed.
  • Data is too high-dimensional to understand directly — a 4D dataset can't be plotted. A 100-feature dataset has billions of possible variable relationships. You need tools to compress the problem.

The Four Core Tasks

TaskWhat it doesExample algorithmsExample use
Clustering Find natural groupings — points in the same cluster are more similar to each other than to any other cluster K-Means, DBSCAN, Hierarchical Customer segments, document topics, user personas
Dimensionality reduction Compress high-dimensional data into fewer dimensions while preserving the most important structure PCA, t-SNE, UMAP, Autoencoders Visualising 100-feature datasets in 2D, removing redundant features before supervised modelling
Anomaly detection Identify points that don't fit the structure the model learned — unusual, rare, or unexpected observations Isolation Forest, One-Class SVM, DBSCAN noise points Fraud detection, equipment failure, data quality checks
Generative modelling Learn the full data distribution P(X) and use it to synthesise new realistic examples VAEs, GANs, Diffusion models Image generation, data augmentation, synthetic data

Unsupervised Learning as a Preprocessing Step

Unsupervised learning doesn't have to stand alone. It is frequently used as a preprocessing or analysis step before supervised modelling — and this is often where it delivers the most practical value.

1. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

Before committing to a supervised approach, use unsupervised methods to understand what's in your data. Clustering can reveal unexpected natural groupings. Dimensionality reduction can expose which features carry the most variance. Anomaly detection surfaces outliers that would distort any model you subsequently train.

Why EDA matters — the dimensionality problem

A dataset with 4 or 5 features already exceeds our ability to visualise directly. At 100+ features, manually exploring all possible relationships is a combinatorial explosion — there are 4,950 possible pairs of features in a 100-feature dataset. Unsupervised learning tools quickly surface the most important structure — which clusters exist, which features co-vary, what the outliers look like — before you commit to a supervised approach.

2. Feature Engineering

Transform raw features into better representations before feeding them to a supervised model. PCA is the classic example — it is technically an unsupervised algorithm (it never sees the labels) but is widely used as a preprocessing step to reduce 500 features down to 20 uncorrelated principal components before training a classifier.

Other examples: learn cluster membership from K-Means and add it as a categorical feature for a downstream regressor. Use an autoencoder's bottleneck representation as input to a neural network classifier.

3. Data Cleaning — Outlier Removal

Anomaly detection as a data quality step: identify and remove or flag unusual points before supervised training. A single outlier can heavily distort a linear regression's coefficients. Running Isolation Forest or DBSCAN as a cleaning step prevents those anomalous points from corrupting the model.

Use caseUnsupervised techniqueRole in pipeline
Understand data before modellingClustering, t-SNEEDA — informs model and feature choices
Reduce feature countPCAPreprocessing — feeds compressed features to supervised model
Add cluster membership as featureK-MeansFeature engineering — enriches the supervised model's inputs
Remove outliers before trainingIsolation Forest, DBSCANData cleaning — prevents distortion of supervised model

Generative Models

A generative model learns the full data distribution P(X) — the probability of observing any given combination of feature values. Once it has learned P(X) it can synthesise new examples by sampling from that distribution. This has exploded with deep learning — image generators, large language models, and music generators are all generative models.

Discriminative vs generative — the key distinction

Discriminative models learn P(Y | X) — given the input, what is the output? They draw a decision boundary. Examples: logistic regression, random forests, SVMs.

Generative models learn P(X) or P(X, Y) — what does the data look like? They model the full distribution. Examples: GANs, VAEs, diffusion models, Naive Bayes.

The difference matters when you want to generate new data, handle missing values, or reason about uncertainty over the inputs — not just classify.

⚠️ Not all generative models are unsupervised. Naive Bayes learns the joint distribution P(X, Y) — including labels — so it is supervised. The defining question is whether labels are used during training, not whether the model can generate data.

The Supervised / Unsupervised Line is Blurry

The same task can often be approached either way depending on what data you have available. Take image denoising as an example:

ApproachTraining data neededHow it learns
SupervisedPairs: (noisy image, clean image)Learns the direct mapping noisy → clean using the label
Unsupervised (autoencoder)Only clean imagesLearns a compressed representation; noise is discarded as irrelevant to the structure

Complex models can also combine both. GANs (Generative Adversarial Networks) are the classic example:

  • The generator is unsupervised — takes random noise and creates synthetic data
  • The discriminator is supervised — classifies inputs as real or fake (a binary label)
  • They train together in competition — the generator gets better at fooling the discriminator, the discriminator gets better at detecting fakes
Self-supervised learning — the middle ground

A growing category that uses the data itself to generate labels automatically. For example, masking a word in a sentence and training the model to predict what word was removed — no human labels, but the training signal comes from the structure of the data. Large language models (GPT, BERT) are trained this way. It behaves like supervised learning mechanically but doesn't require human annotation, making it practically unsupervised.

Real Example: Wikipedia Article Embedding

Take thousands of Wikipedia articles — each described by a high-dimensional vector (word frequencies, topic weights). An unsupervised model compresses each article into a 2D coordinate, placing similar articles near each other in the projected space.

When you plot the result, distinct clusters emerge naturally — science articles cluster together, history articles cluster separately, and so on. When you overlay the actual Wikipedia categories — which were never given to the model — they match the clusters closely.

This validates that the unsupervised model captured real structure. The pattern is common in practice: use unsupervised learning to discover structure, then check against available labels to validate. If they align, the model has found something meaningful.

Evaluating Unsupervised Models

For supervised learning, evaluation is straightforward — compare predictions to correct answers. Unsupervised learning has no correct answers, so evaluation is harder and inherently more task-dependent.

MethodHow it worksWhen to use
Extrinsic evaluation If you happen to have labels, check whether the discovered structure aligns with them. Adjusted Rand Index, Normalised Mutual Information. When labels exist but weren't used in training — validates the model found real categories
Intrinsic metrics Measure structure quality without labels. Silhouette score (how tight are clusters vs how separated), inertia (within-cluster variance). Comparing different K values or algorithm choices on the same dataset
Utility evaluation Does the output make a downstream task better? Does PCA improve the classifier? Do the clusters differ in purchasing behaviour? When unsupervised learning is a preprocessing step — evaluate the end-to-end pipeline
Domain expert review Show the clusters or anomalies to a subject matter expert. Do the groups make sense? Are the flagged outliers genuinely unusual? When the output drives business decisions — human validation is essential
⚠️ There is no single universal metric like accuracy for unsupervised models. A high silhouette score does not mean the clusters are meaningful — it only means they are compact and separated. Always combine quantitative metrics with domain knowledge.

🧪 Quick Check

Unsupervised Learning · L2

🔵 K-Means Clustering

Partitioning data into k groups by iteratively assigning points to the nearest centroid — the most widely used clustering algorithm.

What is K-Means?

K-Means partitions n data points into exactly k clusters. You decide k upfront. Each cluster is defined by its centroid — the mean position of all points assigned to it. Every point belongs to whichever cluster's centroid is nearest to it.

Important: clustering is subjective

There is no single "correct" clustering of a dataset. Different groups of people might group the same objects in perfectly valid but different ways — by colour, by size, by function. K-Means finds the best partition according to its mathematical criterion (inertia), but whether that partition is meaningful is a human judgement. Always interpret clusters in the context of your domain.

Key definitions

TermDefinition
CentroidThe centre of a cluster — the mean of all points assigned to it. It is recalculated after every assignment step
Hard clusteringEach point belongs to exactly one cluster, with no partial membership. K-Means is hard clustering. (Soft/fuzzy clustering allows probabilities)
InertiaThe within-cluster sum of squared distances from each point to its centroid. K-Means minimises this
Silhouette scoreA measure of how well each point fits its cluster vs how close it is to the nearest other cluster. Ranges −1 to +1
Euclidean distanceThe straight-line distance between two points: √((a₁−b₁)² + (a₂−b₂)² + ...). K-Means uses this to assign points to clusters
ConvergenceThe point where no points change their cluster assignment between iterations — the algorithm has found a stable solution
Local optimumA solution that is optimal for a particular random starting position but may not be the globally best solution

Key properties of K-Means

  • Hard clustering — each point belongs to exactly one cluster, no partial membership
  • Flat structure — no hierarchy between clusters (unlike hierarchical clustering)
  • You choose k — the number of clusters must be specified before fitting
  • Sensitive to initialisation — different random starting centroids can give different results
  • Assumes globular shapes — works best when clusters are roughly circular and similar in size

The Algorithm — Step by Step

K-Means alternates between two simple steps until no point changes its cluster assignment (convergence):

StepWhat happensWhy
0. InitialiseRandomly place k centroids in the feature spaceStarting positions — the algorithm needs somewhere to begin
1. AssignEach point is assigned to the nearest centroid using Euclidean distanceEvery point must belong to exactly one cluster at all times
2. UpdateRecalculate each centroid as the mean of all assigned pointsThe centroid must represent the centre of its current members
Repeat 1→2Keep reassigning and recalculating until assignments stop changingEach iteration reduces inertia — the algorithm converges to a stable solution
Why it converges

Each assignment step can only reduce or maintain inertia (every point moves to a nearer centroid). Each update step can only reduce or maintain inertia (the mean is the point that minimises sum of squared distances). Since inertia is always decreasing and has a lower bound of zero, the algorithm must stop. In practice it converges quickly — typically in under 20 iterations.

Euclidean distance — the core calculation

Every assignment decision is based on Euclidean distance. For two points a and b with n dimensions:

D(a, b) = √((a₁−b₁)² + (a₂−b₂)² + ... + (aₙ−bₙ)²)

# Implementation
def euclidean_distance(a, b):
    return sum((a_i - b_i)**2 for a_i, b_i in zip(a, b)) ** 0.5

Each point is assigned to the cluster with the smallest Euclidean distance to the centroid. This is why feature scaling is critical — a feature with values in the thousands will dominate the distance calculation over a feature ranging 0–1, regardless of which feature is actually more informative.

Local optima — why n_init matters

K-Means converges to the nearest local optimum from the random starting point — not necessarily the global best. Different random starts can give very different results, some much worse than others.

# n_init=10: runs K-Means 10 times with different random starting centroids
# Keeps whichever run achieved the lowest inertia
# Always use n_init >= 10 for reliable results
kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=3, n_init=10, random_state=0)
kmeans.fit(data)

Data Preprocessing for K-Means

K-Means is one of the algorithms that is most sensitive to how you prepare your data. Skipping preprocessing is one of the most common causes of poor or misleading clustering results.

1. Feature Scaling — Why it is Essential

K-Means uses Euclidean distance to assign points to clusters. If one feature has values in the thousands and another ranges 0–1, the large-scale feature will dominate every distance calculation — not because it is more important, but purely because of its scale. The algorithm effectively ignores the small-scale features.

The scaling problem — a concrete example

Imagine clustering customers on age (range 18–80) and annual_salary (range £20,000–£200,000). Without scaling, a salary difference of £1,000 has the same effect on distance as an age difference of 1 year. But numerically, salary contributes 1000× more to the distance. Every cluster will be dominated by salary differences — age will be invisible. With scaling, both features contribute equally.

StandardScaler vs MinMaxScaler — which to choose

ScalerFormulaOutput rangeUse when
StandardScaler z = (x − mean) / std Mean=0, Std=1 (unbounded) Features roughly normally distributed. Most common choice for K-Means. Outliers get large z-scores but don't compress other data.
MinMaxScaler x' = (x − min) / (max − min) [0, 1] When you need all features in a fixed range. Sensitive to outliers — one extreme value compresses all other values toward 0.
RobustScaler x' = (x − median) / IQR Centred but unbounded When your data has significant outliers that would distort StandardScaler. Uses median and IQR instead of mean and std. 
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

scaler = StandardScaler()
# fit_transform: learns mean/std from training data AND transforms it
# Always fit on training data only — apply the same transform to new data
customers_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(customers)

# Now fit K-Means on the scaled data
kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=2, n_init=10, random_state=0)
kmeans.fit(customers_scaled)

2. Handle Missing Values

K-Means cannot compute distances when values are missing. You must impute or remove missing data before clustering.

# Option 1: drop rows with any missing values
customers.dropna(inplace=True)

# Option 2: impute with column mean (quick, reasonable for continuous features)
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
imputer = SimpleImputer(strategy='mean')
customers_imputed = imputer.fit_transform(customers)

3. Feature Selection

More features is not always better. Adding irrelevant features adds noise — the algorithm is trying to find clusters in a higher-dimensional space where the extra dimensions add no signal. In practice, use domain knowledge to select features that are relevant to the question you are asking. If you are segmenting customers by spending behaviour, include spending features — not their postcode.

Correlated features also cause problems: if total_spent and mean_spent move together perfectly, including both double-counts that dimension in the distance calculation.

K-Means in sklearn — Standard Workflow

from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
import pandas as pd

# Step 1: Load and select features
customers_data = pd.read_csv('data/retail_dataset.csv', index_col='CustomerID')
features = ['balance', 'max_spent', 'mean_spent', 'min_spent',
            'n_orders', 'total_items', 'total_refunded', 'total_spent']
customers = customers_data[features]

# Step 2: Scale features (critical for K-Means)
scaler = StandardScaler()
customers_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(customers)

# Step 3: Create and fit the model
kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=2, n_init=10, random_state=0)
kmeans.fit(customers_scaled)

# Step 4: Get cluster labels
cluster_assignment = kmeans.predict(customers_scaled)
# → array([0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1, ...])

# Step 5: Inspect centroids (in scaled space)
centers_df = pd.DataFrame(data=kmeans.cluster_centers_, columns=features)
print(centers_df[['mean_spent', 'max_spent']])
Reading standardised centroid values

After StandardScaler, centroid values are in standard deviations from the population mean. 0 = average, +1 = one std above, −1 = one std below.

A centroid at mean_spent = +1.30 means that cluster's typical member spends 1.3 standard deviations more than the average customer — a meaningfully high spender. A centroid at mean_spent = −0.25 is a slightly below-average spender.

Visualising and Interpreting Clusters

Pairplot — seeing all feature combinations

import seaborn as sns

def pairplot_cluster(df, cols, cluster_assignment):
    df_tmp = df.copy()                      # never modify the original
    df_tmp['cluster'] = cluster_assignment  # add labels as a column
    sns.pairplot(df_tmp, vars=cols, hue='cluster')

# 2-feature clustering — boundary visible in 2D
cust2 = customers[['mean_spent', 'max_spent']]
kmeans2 = KMeans(n_clusters=2, n_init=10).fit(cust2)
pairplot_cluster(customers, ['mean_spent', 'max_spent'], kmeans2.predict(cust2))

# All-feature clustering — boundary found in 8D space
kmeans_all = KMeans(n_clusters=2, n_init=10).fit(customers_scaled)
pairplot_cluster(customers, ['mean_spent', 'max_spent'], kmeans_all.predict(customers_scaled))
How to read a pairplot

Diagonal: KDE density curves — the distribution of each feature for each cluster. If the curves for cluster 0 and cluster 1 are well-separated, that feature is a strong differentiator.

Off-diagonal: scatter plots of two features coloured by cluster. Clean separation between colours = well-defined clusters in those two dimensions.

Mixed/overlapping colours in all-feature clustering: this does NOT mean the clustering is wrong. When you cluster on 8 features, the separation exists in 8D space. Plotting any two features collapses 6 dimensions of information — points that are far apart in 8D can appear close in 2D. The clustering is still valid; the 2D plot just can't show the full picture.

Box plot — comparing cluster distributions

cluster0 = customers[cluster_assignment == 0]
cluster1 = customers[cluster_assignment == 1]

sns.boxplot(data=[cluster0.mean_spent, cluster1.mean_spent])
plt.xlabel('Cluster')
plt.ylabel('mean_spent (standardised)')
plt.show()
Box plot elementWhat it showsHow to interpret
Middle lineMedian (50th percentile)The typical value for that cluster on this feature
Box edges25th and 75th percentile (IQR)Where the middle 50% of the cluster sits
WhiskersExtend to furthest non-outlier (1.5 × IQR)The normal range of the cluster
Dots beyond whiskersOutliersUnusual members of the cluster — investigate these
Wide boxHigh spread within clusterThe cluster is heterogeneous on this feature
Narrow boxTight clusterMembers are very similar on this feature

Statistical comparison with describe()

# Compare summary statistics side by side
desc0 = cluster0[['mean_spent', 'max_spent']].describe()
desc1 = cluster1[['mean_spent', 'max_spent']].describe()
compare = desc0.join(desc1, lsuffix='_cluster0', rsuffix='_cluster1')
print(compare)

Inertia — What K-Means Actually Optimises

K-Means minimises inertia — the within-cluster sum of squared distances from each point to its centroid. This is the mathematical objective the algorithm is solving.

The inertia formula

I = Σᵢ Σ_{x∈Cᵢ} D(x, μᵢ)²

For each cluster i: sum the squared Euclidean distance between every point x in that cluster and the cluster's centroid μᵢ. Then sum across all clusters. Lower inertia = tighter, more compact clusters.

print(f'Inertia: {kmeans.inertia_:.2f}')  # available after fitting
⚠️ Inertia has three important limitations:
(1) Not normalised — a raw inertia value of 5,000 tells you nothing on its own. It is only useful for comparing different values of k on the same dataset.
(2) Always decreases with k — adding more clusters always reduces inertia, even if those clusters are meaningless. At k=n, inertia=0 (one point per cluster) — useless.
(3) Assumes globular clusters — inertia works poorly for elongated, irregular, or non-convex cluster shapes because it measures distance to a single mean point.

Choosing k — Elbow Method

Why: You must choose k before fitting. Too few clusters merge genuinely different groups. Too many over-split natural groupings into arbitrary sub-groups. The elbow method helps find the point where adding more clusters stops providing meaningful improvement.

inertias = []
k_vals = range(1, 21)

for k in k_vals:
    km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, n_init=10, random_state=0)
    km.fit(customers_scaled)
    inertias.append(km.inertia_)

plt.plot(k_vals, inertias, marker='s')
plt.xlabel('Number of Clusters (k)')
plt.ylabel('Inertia')
plt.title('Elbow Method')
plt.show()
How to read the elbow plot

Inertia always decreases as k increases — that's expected. Look for the elbow: the point where the rate of decrease changes most sharply. Before the elbow, each additional cluster meaningfully tightens existing clusters. After the elbow, each additional cluster only marginally splits noise.

If the curve is smooth with no clear elbow, the data has no strong natural grouping structure at any specific k — or the elbow is being masked by scale. In that case, use the silhouette score instead.

Choosing k — Silhouette Score

Why: The elbow method is visual and subjective — two people may disagree on where the elbow is. The silhouette score gives a quantitative measure of cluster quality that can be compared directly across different k values.

The silhouette formula: s(i) = (b − a) / max(a, b)

a = mean distance from point i to all other points in its own cluster (cohesion — measures how tightly packed the cluster is around point i)

b = mean distance from point i to all points in the nearest different cluster (separation — measures how far point i is from the wrong cluster)

+1: perfectly placed — tight in its cluster, far from others
0: on the boundary between two clusters
−1: in the wrong cluster — it would fit better somewhere else

from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

k_vals = range(1, 21)
silhouette_scores = []
inertias = []

for k in k_vals:
    km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, n_init=10, random_state=0)
    km.fit(customers_scaled)
    inertias.append(km.inertia_)

    if k > 1:  # silhouette undefined for k=1 (no other cluster to compare)
        labels = km.predict(customers_scaled)
        silhouette_scores.append(silhouette_score(customers_scaled, labels))
    else:
        silhouette_scores.append(None)

best_k = k_vals[silhouette_scores.index(max(s for s in silhouette_scores if s))]
print(f'Best k by silhouette: {best_k}')

Dual plot — inertia and silhouette together

fig, ax1 = plt.subplots()

ax1.set_xlabel('k')
ax1.set_ylabel('Inertia', color='tab:orange')
ax1.plot(k_vals, inertias, color='tab:orange')
ax1.tick_params(axis='y', labelcolor='tab:orange')

ax2 = ax1.twinx()
ax2.set_ylabel('Silhouette Score', color='tab:blue')
ax2.plot(k_vals, silhouette_scores, color='tab:blue')
ax2.tick_params(axis='y', labelcolor='tab:blue')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
How to read the dual plot

Inertia (orange): always decreases. Look for where the rate of decline slows sharply — the elbow.

Silhouette (blue): higher is better. The peak is the best k by this metric.

When both agree: high confidence — that k is almost certainly the right choice.

When they disagree: investigate both candidates. Silhouette is generally more reliable because it directly measures cluster quality rather than just fit tightness. If silhouette has a secondary peak, that suggests there may be meaningful sub-clusters within one of the main clusters worth exploring.

Model Evaluation

Choosing k and computing silhouette is not enough — you also need to validate that the clusters are meaningful, stable, and useful.

MethodWhat it measuresHow to use it
Inertia (elbow) Within-cluster tightness. Always decreases with k. Plot vs k. Use elbow as a candidate k — not a definitive answer.
Silhouette score How well each point fits its cluster vs the nearest rival. Range −1 to +1. Plot vs k. Pick the peak. Above 0.5 = reasonable. Above 0.7 = good. Above 0.85 = excellent separation.
Centroid inspection Whether clusters have different, interpretable characteristics. Print cluster_centers_. If centroids are very similar, the clusters may not be meaningfully different.
Cluster size balance Whether clusters are extremely unequal in size. Check cluster sizes with np.unique(labels, return_counts=True). One giant cluster + many tiny clusters is a red flag.
Stability check Whether the same solution appears across different random seeds. Run K-Means with 5 different random_state values. If results differ dramatically, the clusters are not stable.
Domain validation Whether the clusters make sense given what you know about the data. Show clusters to a domain expert. Do the groupings align with known customer types, behaviour patterns, or categories? 
import numpy as np

# Check cluster sizes
unique, counts = np.unique(cluster_assignment, return_counts=True)
for c, n in zip(unique, counts):
    print(f'Cluster {c}: {n} points ({100*n/len(cluster_assignment):.1f}%)')

# Check silhouette
score = silhouette_score(customers_scaled, cluster_assignment)
print(f'Silhouette: {score:.3f}')

# Interpret
if score > 0.7:   print("Good separation")
elif score > 0.5: print("Reasonable separation")
elif score > 0.25: print("Weak structure — clusters may overlap")
else:             print("Poor structure — consider different k or algorithm")

Pros, Cons, and When to Use K-Means

ProsCons
Fast — scales to millions of pointsMust choose k upfront — no automatic discovery of the number of clusters
Easy to interpret — centroids directly describe each clusterConverges to local optimum — use n_init ≥ 10
Assigning new points is trivial (just find nearest centroid)Assumes globular (circular) cluster shapes — fails on elongated or irregular clusters
Simple to implement and explain to stakeholdersSensitive to outliers — a single extreme point pulls the centroid away from the true cluster centre
Works well when clusters are compact and roughly equal in sizeSensitive to feature scale — must standardise before clustering
Memory-efficient — only stores k centroids after fittingHard clustering — every point gets exactly one label, even ambiguous boundary points

When to use K-Means

  • You have a large dataset and need a fast result
  • You have a rough idea of how many clusters to expect
  • Your clusters are expected to be roughly spherical and similar in size
  • You need interpretable cluster centres (e.g. customer personas, audience segments)
  • You're doing exploratory work and want a quick first pass at the structure of the data

When NOT to use K-Means — and what to use instead

SituationProblemUse instead
Clusters have very different sizesLarge clusters pull centroids; small ones get absorbedDBSCAN, Gaussian Mixture Models
Clusters are elongated or irregular shapesEuclidean distance to centroid doesn't capture non-spherical structureDBSCAN, Spectral Clustering
You don't know k at allMust specify k upfrontDBSCAN (k-free), Hierarchical clustering (cut at any level)
Data has many outliersOutliers distort centroids and inflate inertiaDBSCAN (marks outliers as noise), Median-based clustering
You need soft assignments (probabilities)K-Means gives hard labels onlyGaussian Mixture Models (probabilistic cluster membership)
High-dimensional sparse data (text)Euclidean distance loses meaning in high dimensionsTopic models (LDA), cosine-similarity-based clustering

🧪 Quick Check

Unsupervised Learning · L3

🌳 Hierarchical Clustering

Building a tree of nested clusters — no need to choose k upfront, and the dendrogram reveals multi-level structure in a single run

What is Hierarchical Clustering?

Hierarchical clustering groups data into a tree of nested clusters. Unlike K-Means (which gives flat labels), it produces a complete hierarchy — you can zoom in to see fine sub-groups, or zoom out for a high-level view, all from a single algorithm run. The key output is a dendrogram: a tree diagram showing every merge the algorithm performed.

No need to choose k upfront. K-Means forces you to commit to a number of clusters before running. Hierarchical clustering builds the full tree first — you choose k afterwards by deciding where to "cut" the dendrogram.

Why it matters — real-world use cases

Biology

Phylogenetic trees — species cluster into genera, genera into families. The tree of life is a natural hierarchy discovered by clustering genetic sequences.

E-Commerce

Customer segmentation — "high spenders" sub-cluster into "frequent buyers" and "large single orders". Reveals customer tiers at multiple resolutions simultaneously.

NLP / Text

Document clustering — "sedan" and "SUV" are sub-clusters of "car", which is a sub-cluster of "vehicle". Captures semantic similarity at multiple levels of granularity.

Bioinformatics

Gene expression — genes that respond similarly to stimuli cluster together, revealing co-expression modules and biological pathways from RNA-Seq data.

Flat vs Hierarchical Clusters

Flat — K-Means Hierarchical
Output One label per point Full tree of all possible clusterings
Choose k? Before running After running, by cutting the dendrogram
Cluster relationships None — clusters are independent Full hierarchy — clusters nested inside clusters
Explainability Low — just integer labels High — the dendrogram tells the full story

Two Approaches: Divisive vs Agglomerative

Approach Direction Mechanism In practice
Divisive Top-down ↓ All points in one cluster → split repeatedly Rarely used — searching all possible splits is NP-hard
Agglomerative ✅ Bottom-up ↑ Each point its own cluster → merge the two nearest repeatedly Standard — simple greedy decisions, O(n² log n) with optimisations

Interactive: Agglomerative Clustering Step-by-Step

Six points start as individual clusters. Click Next Step to watch the algorithm merge them from nearest to furthest. Notice the big distance jump between within-cluster and between-cluster merges — that gap is where you should cut the dendrogram.

Step 0/5 — Every point is its own cluster
Cluster A Cluster B Cluster C A+C merged All merged

The Algorithm

  1. Initialise — treat every data point as its own cluster. You have N clusters.
  2. Compute the N×N pairwise distance matrix between all clusters using your chosen metric and linkage.
  3. Find the pair (cᵢ, cⱼ) with the smallest distance.
  4. Merge them into a new combined cluster. Record this merge event (who merged and at what distance).
  5. Update the distance matrix to reflect the new cluster.
  6. If more than one cluster remains → go to step 3. Otherwise stop.

After N−1 merges all points share one cluster. The full history of merges is the dendrogram.

Two Decisions You Must Make

1. Distance Metric — how far apart are two individual points?

MetricFormulaBest for
Euclidean ✅√Σ(xᵢ−yᵢ)²Continuous, well-scaled numeric data (default)
ManhattanΣ|xᵢ−yᵢ|High-dimensional data; less sensitive to outliers
Cosine1 − (x·y)/(‖x‖‖y‖)Text / sparse vectors — direction matters, not magnitude

2. Linkage — how far apart are two multi-point clusters?

Linkage Distance defined as… Weakness
Single Distance between the two nearest points across clusters Chaining — one outlier bridges two distant clusters early
Complete Distance between the two furthest points across clusters One outlier can block a natural merge indefinitely
Average Centroid-to-centroid distance Can push most data into one giant cluster (seen in the practical!)
Ward ✅ Merge that minimises the increase in total within-cluster variance Best default — produces compact, balanced clusters

Interactive: How Different Linkages Measure Distance

The yellow line shows the distance measured between clusters X (blue) and Y (purple). Z (green) is a third cluster for reference. Toggle to see how each linkage method defines inter-cluster distance.

Single linkage: distance = nearest pair. Vulnerable to chaining — one bridge point can incorrectly merge distant groups.

Data Preprocessing for Hierarchical Clustering

Hierarchical clustering is distance-based, making it highly sensitive to scale and data quality. Good preprocessing directly determines cluster quality.

1. Feature Scaling — the most critical step

A feature measured in thousands (e.g. total revenue) will dominate one measured in ones (e.g. number of orders) if you don't scale. Always standardise before clustering.

from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

# StandardScaler: z-score normalisation → mean=0, std=1 (recommended default)
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X)

# MinMaxScaler alternative: scales to [0,1]
# More sensitive to outliers — use StandardScaler unless you have a reason not to

2. Handling Outliers

Why outliers are dangerous in hierarchical clustering

  • Single linkage: one outlier forms a "bridge" between two distant clusters, incorrectly merging them early — the chaining effect
  • Average / Ward: an outlier forces a cluster to merge at an unnaturally high distance, distorting the whole dendrogram

Detect with IQR-based trimming or Isolation Forest. Cap or remove before fitting.

3. Missing Values

from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer

# Impute with column median (robust to outliers)
imputer = SimpleImputer(strategy='median')
X_imputed = imputer.fit_transform(X)

# Or drop rows if missing values are few
df_clean = df.dropna()

4. Dimensionality Reduction (recommended for d > 20)

In high dimensions Euclidean distance loses meaning — all points appear equally far apart. Apply PCA first to reduce noise and speed up clustering.

from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

# Keep 95% of variance
pca = PCA(n_components=0.95)
X_pca = pca.fit_transform(X_scaled)
print(f"Reduced from {X.shape[1]} to {X_pca.shape[1]} dimensions")
# Cluster on X_pca instead of X_scaled

5. Categorical Variables

# Option 1: one-hot encode then scale
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder
enc = OneHotEncoder(sparse_output=False)
X_cat = enc.fit_transform(df[['category_col']])

# Option 2: Gower distance handles mixed types natively
import gower
dist_matrix = gower.gower_matrix(df)   # pip install gower
# Pass the pre-computed distance matrix directly
Z = linkage(dist_matrix, method='average')

When to Use Hierarchical Clustering

Use it when… Avoid it when…
You don't know k and want to explore many values from one run n > 10,000 — O(n²) memory and O(n² log n) time becomes prohibitive
Data has genuine hierarchical structure (taxonomy, geography, ontologies) Many outliers need explicit labelling — use DBSCAN instead
Interpretability matters — dendrograms communicate structure clearly to stakeholders Clusters are non-convex / irregular in shape (rings, crescents)
n is small-to-medium (< 5,000) and you want maximum insight before committing to k You need to classify new incoming data — no predict() for new points

Implementation

scipy — build the full hierarchy

from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import linkage, dendrogram
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

X_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(customers[features])

# linkage() returns a matrix Z of shape (n-1, 4)
# Each row: [cluster_a, cluster_b, merge_distance, new_cluster_size]
Z = linkage(X_scaled, method='ward', metric='euclidean')

plt.figure(figsize=(18, 6))
dendrogram(Z)
plt.ylabel('Ward Distance')
plt.xlabel('Sample index')
plt.show()

sklearn — get flat cluster labels

from sklearn.cluster import AgglomerativeClustering

model = AgglomerativeClustering(
    n_clusters=3,       # cut the tree to produce 3 clusters
    linkage='ward',
    metric='euclidean'
)
labels = model.fit_predict(X_scaled)
# labels: array of shape (n,) — values 0, 1, ..., k-1
# Note: no predict() method for new data — must refit on the full dataset

Dendrograms — How to Read Them

  • Y-axis (height): the distance at which two groups merged. Taller bar = more different groups joining.
  • Horizontal bar: one merge event. Its height is the distance between the two sub-trees being joined.
  • Tall vertical gap before a bar: a strong natural cluster boundary — this is where you should cut.
  • X-axis: individual point indices, or (n) = a cluster of size n after truncation.

Interactive: Adjust the Cut Height to Choose k

Drag the slider left and right. The red dashed line is the cut — every vertical branch it crosses becomes one cluster. Notice how the big gap between heights 30 and 110 makes 3 clusters the most natural choice.

Low cut High cut
Cut at height 80 → 3 clusters

Truncation — simplifying large dendrograms

plt.figure(figsize=(18, 6))
dendrogram(
    Z,
    truncate_mode='lastp',  # keep only the last p non-singleton nodes
    p=20,                   # show the 20 most recent merges
    color_threshold=5.0     # colour all branches below this height the same
)
plt.ylabel('Ward Distance')
plt.xlabel('Sample or (cluster size)')
# (83) = 83 customers merged at this node; 42 = individual customer #42
plt.show()

Evaluation Methods

No single "correct" answer exists — use multiple metrics together and combine with domain knowledge.

1. Dendrogram Gap Analysis (visual)

The most important diagnostic. Find the largest vertical gap before a horizontal bar. A large gap means the two sub-trees being merged were genuinely dissimilar — a natural cluster boundary. Cut just below it.

2. Silhouette Score

Measures how similar each point is to its own cluster vs the nearest other cluster. Ranges −1 (misassigned) to +1 (well-assigned). Aim for > 0.5.

from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

for k in range(2, 9):
    labels = AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=k, linkage='ward').fit_predict(X_scaled)
    score = silhouette_score(X_scaled, labels)
    print(f"k={k}: silhouette = {score:.3f}")
# k=3: silhouette = 0.512  ← choose the highest value

3. Cophenetic Correlation Coefficient

Measures how faithfully the dendrogram preserves original pairwise distances. Closer to 1.0 = better. Above 0.75 is generally good; below 0.6 suggests the chosen linkage is a poor fit for the data.

from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import cophenet
from scipy.spatial.distance import pdist

Z = linkage(X_scaled, method='ward', metric='euclidean')
c, _ = cophenet(Z, pdist(X_scaled))
print(f"Cophenetic correlation: {c:.4f}")
# 0.85+ → excellent; 0.6–0.85 → acceptable; < 0.6 → consider a different linkage

4. Elbow Method — Average Within-Cluster Variance

Plot average within-cluster variance vs k. The "elbow" is where adding more clusters stops reducing variance significantly. Confirmed by the practical: the elbow at k=2 or 3 matches the visual dendrogram gap.

def cluster_variance(points):
    N = points.shape[0]
    if N < 2: return 0
    total = sum(0.5 * np.linalg.norm(points[i] - points[j])**2
                for i in range(N) for j in range(N))
    return total / (N**2)

avg_vars = []
for k in range(1, 11):
    labels = AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=k, linkage='ward').fit_predict(X_scaled)
    avg_vars.append(np.mean([cluster_variance(X_scaled[labels==c]) for c in np.unique(labels)]))

plt.plot(range(1, 11), avg_vars, marker='o', color='#5b8af5')
plt.xlabel('k'); plt.ylabel('Average Within-Cluster Variance')
plt.axvline(x=3, color='#f87171', linestyle='--', label='Elbow at k=3')
plt.legend(); plt.show()

Real-World Example: Customer Segmentation

From the practical notebook, using an Online Retail dataset of ~4,000 customers with features: total spend, order frequency, average basket size, refunds.

Key finding: linkage method has a huge impact

# Average linkage first — reveals the imbalance problem
Z_avg = linkage(customers, method='average', metric='euclidean')
dendrogram(Z_avg)
# → One enormous cluster + a few singletons. Nearly useless for segmentation.

# Switch to Ward — produces three balanced, interpretable segments
Z_ward = linkage(customers, method='ward', metric='euclidean')
dendrogram(Z_ward, truncate_mode='lastp', p=20, color_threshold=70)
# → Three clearly distinct super-clusters visible in the dendrogram
Practical lesson: Average linkage pushed nearly all customers into one massive cluster. Ward linkage produced three balanced, meaningful segments. Always try multiple linkage methods and compare dendrograms before committing.

Profiling the clusters

model = AgglomerativeClustering(n_clusters=3, linkage='ward', metric='euclidean')
customers['cluster'] = model.fit_predict(customers[features])

# Profile each cluster
print(customers.groupby('cluster')[features].mean().round(2))
# cluster 0: low total_spent, high n_orders → "frequent bargain shoppers"
# cluster 1: high total_spent, low n_orders → "occasional big spenders"
# cluster 2: medium spend + orders → "mid-tier regulars"

# Visualise separation
sns.pairplot(customers, vars=['mean_spent', 'max_spent', 'n_orders'], hue='cluster')
plt.show()

# Compare to true labels (Iris example) — side by side
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4), sharey=True, sharex=True)
axs[0].scatter(X[:,0], X[:,1], c=y_true);  axs[0].set_title('True Labels')
axs[1].scatter(X[:,0], X[:,1], c=labels);  axs[1].set_title('Hierarchical k=3')
# Colours won't match — numbering is arbitrary. The SHAPE of groupings is what matters.

Pros and Cons

✅ Pros ❌ Cons
No need to choose k upfront — explore all values from one dendrogram Slow for large n — O(n² log n) time, O(n²) memory
Dendrogram reveals structure at every resolution in one interpretable plot Cannot predict cluster for new data — must refit the whole model
Finds naturally hierarchical structure (biology, geography, language) Early merges are irreversible — a bad local decision propagates upward
Fully deterministic — same result every run, no random seed issues Struggles in high dimensions — distances become uniform (curse of dimensionality)
Intuitive dendrogram output — easy to explain to non-technical audiences Assumes convex cluster shapes — rings or crescents will be split incorrectly
Rule of thumb: For n < 5,000 where interpretability matters, hierarchical clustering with Ward linkage is an excellent first choice. For n > 10,000, or when you need to classify new incoming data, use K-Means or DBSCAN instead.

🧪 Quick Check

Unsupervised Learning · L4

🔵 DBSCAN

Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise — finds clusters of any shape, requires no k upfront, and explicitly identifies outliers

Why DBSCAN?

K-Means and Hierarchical clustering share two hard limitations that DBSCAN was designed to fix:

Problem 1: Forced cluster assignment

K-Means and Hierarchical silently absorb every point into a cluster — even genuine outliers. There is no way to say "this point doesn't belong anywhere."

Problem 2: Shape assumptions

Both algorithms assume roughly spherical (blob-shaped) clusters. Rings, crescents, and elongated shapes get incorrectly split into blobs.

DBSCAN's solution: define clusters as dense regions of space, separated from other clusters by sparse regions. This allows any shape, explicitly labels genuine outliers as noise (−1), and requires no k upfront.

Real-world use cases

Anomaly Detection

Fraud detection — fraudulent transactions form sparse outliers (noise = −1) isolated from the dense cluster of normal behaviour. DBSCAN flags them automatically.

Geospatial

Urban hotspot analysis — city districts, traffic accident clusters, and epidemic outbreak zones form irregular geographic shapes that K-Means cannot capture.

Image Analysis

Satellite imagery segmentation — forests, water bodies, and urban areas have irregular, non-convex boundaries. DBSCAN traces their true shapes.

Finance

Credit card behaviour clustering — the practical dataset shows DBSCAN identifying a dense "normal usage" cluster with genuine outlier spenders explicitly labelled as noise.

The 2 Parameters

ParameterWhat it controlsToo smallToo large
eps (ε) Search radius — how far to look for neighbours Most points become noise Everything merges into one cluster
min_samples Density threshold — minimum neighbours (including self) to be considered dense Everything becomes a core point — noisy clusters Too few cores — most points become noise

Starting rules of thumb

  • min_samples: start at 2 × number of features. For 17 features (credit card data) → min_samples = 34. Increase for noisier data.
  • eps: plot the nearest-neighbour distance distribution and pick a value in the right tail — where the histogram starts thinning out.

The 3 Point Types

Given eps and min_samples, every point gets exactly one classification:

Type Definition Role
● Core point Has ≥ min_samples points (including itself) within radius eps Can start and extend a cluster
● Border point Fewer than min_samples neighbours, but within eps of a core point Belongs to a cluster but cannot extend it
✕ Noise point Not within eps of any core point — genuinely isolated Label = −1

Interactive: DBSCAN Parameter Explorer

Adjust eps and min_samples to see how every point gets classified in real time. Core points (blue) have enough dense neighbours; border points (amber) are near a core; noise points (red ×) are isolated.

● Core: 0 ● Border: 0 ✕ Noise: 0 Clusters found: 0
Tip: try eps=40, min_samples=4 for 2 clean clusters. Try eps=110 to see them merge. Try eps=15 to see almost everything become noise.

How Clusters Form: Reachability

  • Directly reachable: point q is within eps of core point p → q is directly reachable from p
  • Reachable: there is a chain of directly-reachable steps from p to q (all intermediate points must be core points)
  • Connected: p and q are density-connected if there exists a point o such that both p and q are reachable from o
  • Cluster: the maximal set of density-connected points

Key insight: border points belong to a cluster but cannot extend it — they terminate the chain. A point initially labelled noise can later be absorbed if a core point's expansion reaches it.

The Algorithm

  1. Pick any unvisited point p. Mark it visited.
  2. Count all points within distance eps of p (including p itself).
  3. If count ≥ min_samples → p is a core point → start a new cluster. Add all eps-neighbours to the cluster. For each neighbour that is also a core point, recursively expand.
  4. If count < min_samples and p is not reachable from any core → mark p as noise (−1).
  5. Repeat until all points are visited.

No random initialisation — algorithm is fully deterministic. Order of point visits can affect border point assignments but not cluster structure.

Interactive: DBSCAN vs K-Means on Non-Convex Data

The most dramatic difference between DBSCAN and K-Means is on non-convex cluster shapes. Below: an outer ring and an inner blob. K-Means (k=2) splits the ring down the middle; DBSCAN finds the true structure. Toggle to compare.

DBSCAN (eps=48, min_samples=3): correctly identifies the inner blob as one cluster and the outer ring as another. Noise points (×) are genuine outliers.

Data Preprocessing

DBSCAN uses Euclidean distance for its epsilon neighbourhood checks, so preprocessing choices directly control which points are classified as core, border, or noise.

1. Feature Scaling — mandatory

Without scaling, features with large magnitudes (e.g. £40,000 credit limit) dominate distance calculations over smaller features (e.g. 0–1 frequency scores). Always scale before fitting DBSCAN.

from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

scaler = StandardScaler()
X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(df)          # z-score: mean=0, std=1
# Fit on train, transform train and any future data separately

2. Missing Values

# Drop rows with missing values (if < 5% of dataset)
df.dropna(inplace=True)

# Or impute with median before scaling
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
X_imputed = SimpleImputer(strategy='median').fit_transform(X)

3. Handling Skewed / Outlier-Heavy Columns

The credit card practical had extreme outliers (max purchases = £49,039 vs mean = £1,025). Binning skewed columns to categories and replacing with medians reduced the outlier effect:

# Bin a skewed column into 6 value ranges, then replace with median of each bin
def bin_to_median(series):
    bins = [0, 500, 1000, 3000, 5000, 10000, float('inf')]
    labels = range(len(bins)-1)
    binned = pd.cut(series, bins=bins, labels=labels, include_lowest=True)
    for b in labels:
        med = series[binned == b].median()
        series = series.mask(binned == b, med)
    return series

skewed_cols = ['BALANCE','PURCHASES','CASH_ADVANCE','CREDIT_LIMIT','PAYMENTS']
for col in skewed_cols:
    df[col] = bin_to_median(df[col])

4. Dimensionality Reduction (recommended for d > 15)

In high dimensions all pairwise distances converge to similar values — eps becomes meaningless. Apply PCA first:

from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

pca = PCA(n_components=0.95)        # keep 95% of variance
X_pca = pca.fit_transform(X_scaled)
# Then run DBSCAN on X_pca (typically much fewer dimensions)

Choosing eps — the KNN Distance Plot

Before fitting, measure how far each point is from its nearest neighbour. The right tail of this distribution shows where density transitions from "dense cluster" to "sparse noise region" — that is your starting eps.

from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import pairwise_distances
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Compute n×n pairwise distance matrix (n=8,636 → ~74M calculations)
all_distances = pairwise_distances(X_scaled, metric='euclidean')

# For each point, the distance to its nearest neighbour (exclude self = 0)
neig_distances = [np.min(row[np.nonzero(row)]) for row in all_distances]

plt.hist(neig_distances, bins=100, density=True)
plt.xlabel('Distance to nearest neighbour')
plt.ylabel('Density')
plt.title('KNN Distance Distribution — pick eps in the right tail')
plt.axvline(x=2.0, color='red', linestyle='--', label='candidate eps=2.0')
plt.legend()
plt.show()
O(n²) warning: pairwise_distances computes all n×n distances. For 8,636 points → ~74M calculations — fine. For 100k+ points, use sklearn.neighbors.NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=2).fit(X) instead — it only finds the k nearest neighbours, not all pairwise distances.

Full sklearn Workflow

Credit card customer clustering (from the practical)

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import pairwise_distances

# ── 1. Load data ─────────────────────────────────────────────
df = pd.read_csv('CC GENERAL.csv').drop('CUST_ID', axis=1)
df.dropna(inplace=True)   # drop 314 rows with missing MINIMUM_PAYMENTS

# ── 2. Scale ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
X_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(df)

# ── 3. Find eps via nearest-neighbour distances ───────────────
all_d = pairwise_distances(X_scaled, metric='euclidean')
neig_d = [np.min(row[np.nonzero(row)]) for row in all_d]
# Inspect histogram → right tail starts around eps=2.0

# ── 4. Fit DBSCAN ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# Rule of thumb: min_samples = 2 × features = 2 × 17 = 34
db = DBSCAN(eps=2, min_samples=34)
labels = db.fit_predict(X_scaled)

# ── 5. Summarise ─────────────────────────────────────────────
n_clusters = len(set(labels)) - (1 if -1 in labels else 0)
n_noise = (labels == -1).sum()
print(f"Clusters: {n_clusters},  Noise: {n_noise} ({n_noise/len(labels)*100:.1f}%)")
# → Clusters: 1,  Noise: X   (initial params often give 1 big cluster + noise)

# ── 6. Visualise via PCA ──────────────────────────────────────
X_2d = PCA(n_components=2).fit_transform(X_scaled)
plt.scatter(X_2d[:,0], X_2d[:,1], c=labels, s=5, cmap='tab10')
plt.colorbar(label='Cluster  (−1 = noise)')
plt.title('DBSCAN on credit card data (PCA projection)')
plt.show()
Practical finding: With initial params (eps=2, min_samples=34) on the full 17-feature dataset, DBSCAN found 1 cluster + noise. Switching to outlier-handled data (binned columns, eps=1.1) revealed 5 meaningful clusters — demonstrating how sensitive results are to preprocessing and parameter choice.

Using PCA to improve clustering in high dimensions

# Apply PCA first, then DBSCAN on the 2D projection
pca = PCA(n_components=2)
X_principal = pca.fit_transform(X_scaled)

# The 2D PCA space is denser than the 17D space, so eps needs to be smaller
db_pca = DBSCAN(eps=2, min_samples=34)
pca_labels = db_pca.fit_predict(X_principal)

print(np.unique(pca_labels))
# → Typically assigns nearly all points to one cluster (PCA space is denser)

# On outlier-handled data with eps=1.1: finds 5 clusters
db2 = DBSCAN(eps=1.1, min_samples=34)
labels2 = db2.fit_predict(scaled_cat_df)
print(pd.Series(labels2).value_counts())
# cluster 0: 3794 | cluster 2: 137 | cluster 4: 58 | noise(-1): 4563

Evaluation Methods

DBSCAN outputs vary widely with parameters. Use multiple signals to assess quality.

1. Noise fraction — a key diagnostic

Too many noise points (>50%) suggests eps is too small. Too few (<1%) suggests eps is too large and outliers are being absorbed into clusters.

noise_fraction = (labels == -1).sum() / len(labels)
print(f"Noise fraction: {noise_fraction:.1%}")
# Aim for a noise fraction that makes domain sense
# For fraud detection: 5–15% noise may be expected
# For customer segmentation: <20% noise is usually appropriate

2. Silhouette Score (excluding noise)

from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

# Exclude noise points — they have no cluster to compare against
mask = labels != -1
if mask.sum() > 1 and len(set(labels[mask])) > 1:
    score = silhouette_score(X_scaled[mask], labels[mask])
    print(f"Silhouette (non-noise): {score:.3f}")
# > 0.5 = good separation; < 0.25 = clusters overlap heavily

3. Parameter sensitivity — sweep eps

for eps in [0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0]:
    lbl = DBSCAN(eps=eps, min_samples=34).fit_predict(X_scaled)
    nc = len(set(lbl)) - (1 if -1 in lbl else 0)
    nn = (lbl==-1).sum()
    print(f"eps={eps:.1f}: {nc} clusters, {nn} noise ({nn/len(lbl)*100:.0f}%)")
# Watch for the "knee" where cluster count stabilises

DBSCAN vs K-Means vs Hierarchical

K-Means Hierarchical DBSCAN
Need k upfront? Yes No (cut dendrogram) No
Cluster shapes Spherical only Ward ≈ spherical Any shape
Handles outliers? Silently absorbs Silently absorbs Labels as −1
Deterministic? No (random init) Yes Yes
Speed O(n·k·t) — fast O(n² log n) O(n²) naive; O(n log n) with index
Best for Known k, clean blobs, large n Exploration, taxonomy, small n Irregular shapes, anomaly detection, noisy data

HDBSCAN — the Next Step

Hierarchical DBSCAN

DBSCAN's biggest weakness is that a single global eps cannot handle clusters of varying density — it either misses sparse clusters or merges dense ones. HDBSCAN fixes this by running DBSCAN at all eps values simultaneously and extracting the most stable clusters.

  • Only one meaningful parameter: min_cluster_size
  • Handles clusters of different densities in the same dataset
  • Available in sklearn ≥ 1.3: sklearn.cluster.HDBSCAN
from sklearn.cluster import HDBSCAN

hdb = HDBSCAN(min_cluster_size=50, min_samples=5)
labels = hdb.fit_predict(X_scaled)
# Soft clustering also available: hdb.probabilities_ gives membership confidence

Pros and Cons

✅ Pros ❌ Cons
No k needed — cluster count emerges from the data eps and min_samples are hard to tune without domain knowledge
Finds clusters of any shape — rings, crescents, elongated blobs Struggles with clusters of varying density — one eps cannot fit all (use HDBSCAN)
Explicitly marks outliers as −1 — great for anomaly detection O(n²) pairwise distances — slow for n > 50,000 without a spatial index
Fully deterministic — same result on every run Must scale features before running — eps is distance-sensitive
Robust to outliers — they don't pull cluster centroids off-centre High dimensions: all distances become similar (curse of dimensionality) — apply PCA first
Rule of thumb: Use DBSCAN when you suspect irregular cluster shapes, have known outliers to detect, or want the number of clusters to emerge from the data. For n > 50,000, use a spatial index (algorithm='ball_tree' or 'kd_tree' in sklearn) or switch to HDBSCAN.

🧪 Quick Check

Unsupervised Learning · L5

🌀 t-SNE

t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbour Embedding — nonlinear dimensionality reduction for visualising high-dimensional data.

Why t-SNE?

Real-world datasets often have hundreds or thousands of features. You cannot plot 500 dimensions — but you can ask: what does this data look like if we compress it to 2D while keeping similar things close together?

PCA answers this linearly — it projects along the axes of maximum variance. But many datasets have nonlinear structure (curves, manifolds, clusters of irregular shapes) that PCA flattens and loses.

t-SNE is a nonlinear dimensionality reduction method that compresses high-dimensional data to 2 or 3 dimensions for visualisation, preserving the local neighbourhood structure of the original data.

Core Idea

Convert distances between points into probabilities. Points that are close in high-D space have a high probability of being neighbours. Find a 2D layout where those same neighbourhood probabilities are reproduced as faithfully as possible.

The 3-Step Algorithm

Step 1 — Probabilities in high-dimensional space

For every pair of points, compute how "close" they are using a Gaussian (bell curve) centred on each point:

# Conceptually: how likely is j to be a neighbour of i?
# p(j|i) = exp(-distance(i,j)² / 2σ²) / sum of all neighbour distances from i
#
# Nearby points → high probability
# Far-away points → near zero
#
# σ (width of bell curve) is set by the perplexity parameter

# Then symmetrised:
# p(i,j) = (p(j|i) + p(i|j)) / 2N

Step 2 — Probabilities in 2D space

In the 2D output, t-SNE uses a Student t-distribution (not Gaussian) to model distances:

# q(i,j) = (1 + ||y_i - y_j||²)⁻¹ / sum of all pairs
Why t-distribution instead of Gaussian?

The t-distribution has heavier tails than a Gaussian. When compressing from 500D to 2D, there is far less space — a Gaussian would crowd dissimilar points too close together (the crowding problem). The t-distribution's heavy tail allows dissimilar points to be placed much further apart, giving clusters room to breathe.

Step 3 — Minimise the mismatch

Measure the difference between the high-D probabilities (p) and the 2D probabilities (q) using KL divergence, then minimise with gradient descent:

# KL(P‖Q) = Σ p(i,j) × log( p(i,j) / q(i,j) )
#
# Minimised iteratively — the 2D points are moved until the
# neighbourhood structure matches the original as closely as possible

The cost function is non-convex — gradient descent can converge to different solutions. This is why t-SNE is non-deterministic. Always set random_state.

Perplexity — The Key Parameter

Perplexity controls how many neighbours each point considers as "local". It sets the σ width of the Gaussian in Step 1.

PerplexityEffect
Too small (< 5)Only looks at nearest neighbours — finds spurious local clumps, structure appears that doesn't really exist
Good range (5–50)Balances local and global structure — clusters meaningful
Too large (> 100)Considers too many neighbours — misses local structure, clusters blend
Default: 30Good starting point for most datasets
Rule of thumb

Denser or larger datasets → higher perplexity. Always try multiple perplexity values and compare — if a pattern only appears at one specific perplexity, treat it with suspicion.

sklearn Code

from sklearn.manifold import TSNE
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# 1. Scale the data
X_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)

# 2. Optional but recommended: PCA to ~50 dims first
#    t-SNE is slow on 500+ features — PCA makes it tractable
#    50 PCA components typically retain 80%+ of variance
X_50 = PCA(n_components=50).fit_transform(X_scaled)

# 3. Run t-SNE
tsne = TSNE(n_components=2, perplexity=30, random_state=42)
X_2d = tsne.fit_transform(X_50)

# 4. Plot — colour by known labels (if available) to validate
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
plt.scatter(X_2d[:, 0], X_2d[:, 1], c=labels, cmap='tab10', s=5)
plt.colorbar(label='Class label')
plt.title('t-SNE visualisation')
plt.axis('off')  # axes have no meaning in t-SNE
plt.show()

Try multiple perplexity values

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(20, 5))

for ax, perp in zip(axes, [5, 30, 50, 100]):
    tsne = TSNE(n_components=2, perplexity=perp, random_state=42)
    X_2d = tsne.fit_transform(X_50)
    ax.scatter(X_2d[:, 0], X_2d[:, 1], c=labels, cmap='tab10', s=5)
    ax.set_title(f'Perplexity = {perp}')
    ax.axis('off')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

t-SNE vs PCA

PCAt-SNE
TypeLinearNonlinear
PreservesGlobal variance / spreadLocal neighbourhood structure
Best forFeature reduction, preprocessing, pipelinesVisualisation and exploration only
Transform new data?Yes — pca.transform(X_new)No — must refit from scratch
SpeedVery fastSlow — O(n²)
Deterministic?YesNo — different each run
Axes interpretable?Yes (% variance explained)No — axes mean nothing
Best practice: PCA then t-SNE

For high-dimensional data (images, genomics, NLP embeddings), always run PCA first to reduce to ~50 components, then run t-SNE on those 50. PCA is fast and removes noise; t-SNE then finds the fine-grained neighbourhood structure. The standard pipeline for things like MNIST (784 pixels → 50 PCA → 2D t-SNE).

Is t-SNE Only for Visualisation?

Primarily yes — but there are a few legitimate additional uses:

UseHow
Cluster discoverySpot apparent groupings in the t-SNE plot, then validate with K-Means or DBSCAN on the original data. t-SNE suggests where to look — not confirms.
Anomaly detection (visual)Isolated points far from all clusters are candidates for outliers. Not rigorous, but useful as a first pass.
Evaluating model representationsExtract learned embeddings from a neural network or autoencoder, then t-SNE them. Clean separated blobs = the model learned meaningful structure.
Why t-SNE cannot be used as a preprocessing step

Unlike PCA, there is no tsne.transform(X_new). The algorithm optimises positions for the training points only — there is no formula to project a new point into the existing layout. Every call to fit_transform produces a potentially different layout. This makes t-SNE unsuitable as a feature reduction step before a classifier.

Critical Limitations — What t-SNE Does NOT Tell You

What you seeWhat it actually means
Axis positions (x=3.4, y=-1.2)Nothing — axes have no interpretable meaning
Cluster sizes (one blob bigger than another)Nothing about real density — t-SNE focuses on local topology, not global scale
Distances between clustersNot reliable — the gap between two clusters in 2D does not represent their distance in the original space
Tiny sub-clusters within a blobMay be real or may be artefacts from low perplexity — always check with multiple perplexity values
UMAP — the modern alternative

UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection) is a newer algorithm with similar goals but faster (scales better to large data), can transform new points, and preserves more global structure. Available via pip install umap-learn → from umap import UMAP. Increasingly preferred over t-SNE in practice.
