Neural Networks & Deep Learning · L1

🧠 Neural Network Fundamentals

From a single artificial neuron to deep multi-layer networks — understanding what makes neural networks the most powerful class of machine learning models ever built

The Problem with Traditional ML

Every ML algorithm you've learned so far — linear regression, decision trees, SVMs, random forests — has one thing in common: you decide what the model looks at. You engineer features, choose representations, and hand the model a pre-processed table of numbers.

This is called feature engineering, and it has a hard ceiling:

For a raw photo (224×224 pixels)

There are 150,528 pixel values. Which combinations mean "cat"? You'd need thousands of hand-crafted rules — and they'd break on slightly different lighting, angles, or breeds.

For a sentence of text

"The bank was steep" vs "The bank was closed" — same word, different meaning. Manually encoding language rules for billions of sentences is impossible.

Neural networks' breakthrough: they do representation learning — they learn which features matter, directly from raw data. You show a neural network a million cat photos, and it discovers its own definition of "cat" from pixel patterns. No feature engineering required.

Why Neural Networks Are So Powerful

Computer Vision

AlexNet (2012) cut the ImageNet error rate from 26% to 15% in one year. By 2017, ResNets reached 3.5% — better than humans. Tasks: classification, object detection, segmentation, medical imaging.

Natural Language

GPT-4, Gemini, Claude — all transformer-based neural networks. Translation, summarisation, question answering, code generation. GPT-4 passes medical licensing exams at the 90th percentile.

Games & Strategy

AlphaGo (2016) beat the world Go champion. AlphaFold (2021) solved protein structure prediction — a 50-year-old biology problem. DeepMind's Atari agents beat humans on 57 games.

Generative AI

Stable Diffusion, DALL-E 3, Midjourney — generate photorealistic images from text. WaveNet generates human-quality speech. Sora generates videos from text descriptions.

The Universal Approximation Theorem

A neural network with one hidden layer and enough neurons can approximate any continuous mathematical function to arbitrary precision.

This is why neural networks are called universal approximators. Whatever mapping exists between your inputs and outputs — no matter how complex or non-linear — a sufficiently large neural network can learn it. The theorem proves the representational capacity exists. The challenge is figuring out how to train it.

Biological Inspiration: The Real Neuron

Biological Neuron Artificial Neuron
Dendrites — receive electrical signals from other neurons Inputs x₁, x₂, x₃ — numerical values fed into the neuron
Synaptic weights — some connections are stronger than others Weights w₁, w₂, w₃ — learned numbers controlling each input's influence
Cell body — sums all incoming signals Weighted sum z = w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + w₃x₃ + b
Threshold — fires only if signal exceeds threshold Activation function f(z) — determines if/how strongly the neuron "fires"
Axon — carries the output signal to the next neuron Output a = f(z) — the activation, passed to the next layer

The Artificial Neuron — How It Works

A single neuron performs two operations:

Step 1: Weighted Sum

z = w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + ... + wₙxₙ + b

z is called the pre-activation or logit. Each input xᵢ is multiplied by its weight wᵢ and summed. The bias b shifts the result — it lets the neuron "fire" even when all inputs are zero.

Step 2: Activation Function

a = f(z)

a is the activation — what the neuron outputs to the next layer. Without f, stacking neurons is useless (a chain of linear operations is still linear). f introduces the non-linearity that makes neural networks powerful.

Interactive: Build and Fire a Neuron

Adjust the inputs and weights to see how they combine into the pre-activation z, and how the chosen activation function transforms z into the final output a. Watch how changing the activation function completely changes the output range.

Activation Functions — The Heart of Non-Linearity

Without an activation function, stacking 100 linear layers is mathematically equivalent to a single linear layer. The activation function f(z) breaks this equivalence by introducing a non-linearity after every neuron — this is what gives neural networks their expressive power.

Interactive: Activation Function Explorer

Toggle between activation functions. The solid line is f(z), the dashed line is the derivative f'(z) — the gradient available for learning. Notice how sigmoid and tanh saturate (gradient → 0) at the extremes, causing the vanishing gradient problem.

ReLU Formula: Output range:

Which activation function should I use?

LayerRecommendedWhy
Hidden layers (default)ReLUFast, no vanishing gradient, simple
Hidden layers (if dying ReLU)Leaky ReLU / ELUNever fully dead neurons
Output — binary classificationSigmoidOutput = probability ∈ (0,1)
Output — multi-classSoftmaxOutput = probability distribution summing to 1
Output — regressionLinear (none)Output can be any real number

Multi-Layer Networks: How Depth Creates Power

A single neuron is just a glorified linear equation. The real power comes from stacking neurons into layers and layers into a network:

    Input        Hidden Layer 1     Hidden Layer 2      Output
    x₁ ─────┐    [●][●][●][●]       [●][●][●]           [ŷ₁]
    x₂ ─────┤──→ [●][●][●][●]  ──→ [●][●][●]  ──────→  [ŷ₂]
    x₃ ─────┤    [●][●][●][●]       [●][●][●]           [ŷ₃]
    x₄ ─────┘    [●][●][●][●]
                   ↑                   ↑                   ↑
              4 neurons each       3 neurons          3 output classes
              + ReLU activation    + ReLU             + Softmax

Input Layer

One node per feature. No computation — just passes raw data. 28×28 pixel image = 784 input nodes.

Hidden Layers

Where all learning happens. Each neuron connects to every neuron in the previous layer (fully-connected / Dense). The network learns hierarchical features: edges → shapes → objects.

Output Layer

Activation matches the task. Regression → linear. Binary → sigmoid. Multi-class → softmax (outputs sum to 1, interpretable as probabilities).

How many weights are there?

A fully-connected layer from 4 inputs to 8 neurons has 4×8 = 32 weights + 8 biases = 40 parameters. GPT-4 has ~1.76 trillion parameters. Every single one is updated via backpropagation during training.

Forward Propagation — Making a Prediction

Forward propagation is how the network turns inputs into a prediction. It passes data through the network layer by layer. For each layer l:

Z[l] = W[l] · A[l-1] + b[l]    # Linear: weighted sum + bias (matrix multiplication)
A[l] = f(Z[l])                  # Non-linear: apply activation function

# Where:
# W[l] = weight matrix, shape [neurons_in_l, neurons_in_l-1]
# A[l-1] = activations from previous layer (= X for layer 1)
# b[l] = bias vector
# f = activation function (ReLU for hidden, softmax for output)

Interactive: Watch Data Flow Through a Network

Adjust the two inputs and watch activations propagate through the 3-layer network in real time. Brighter/bigger neurons = stronger activation. Follow a signal from input to prediction.

Architecture: 2 → 3 → 2 → 1 | Hidden: ReLU | Output: Sigmoid | Values shown inside neurons

Loss Functions — Measuring How Wrong We Are

After forward propagation gives a prediction ŷ, the loss function measures how wrong it is. Training = minimising this number.

TaskLoss FunctionFormulaWhy
RegressionMSE(1/n)Σ(y − ŷ)²Penalises large errors heavily
Binary classificationBinary Cross-Entropy−[y·log(ŷ)+(1−y)·log(1−ŷ)]Perfect for probability outputs
Multi-classCategorical Cross-Entropy−Σ yᵢ·log(ŷᵢ)Works with softmax output
Cross-entropy intuition: if the true class is 1 and you predict probability 0.99 → loss = −log(0.99) ≈ 0.01 (tiny). Predict 0.01 → loss = −log(0.01) ≈ 4.6 (huge penalty). The log punishes confident wrong predictions most severely.

Backpropagation — How Networks Learn

Forward propagation gives you a prediction and a loss. But which of the millions of weights caused the error? Backpropagation answers this using the chain rule of calculus — it computes how much each weight contributed to the loss.

The Chain Rule — propagating blame backwards

∂L/∂w = ∂L/∂a · ∂a/∂z · ∂z/∂w

  • ∂L/∂a — how much the loss changes when the activation changes (from the layer above)
  • ∂a/∂z — the derivative of the activation function (ReLU's = 1 or 0; sigmoid's = s(1−s))
  • ∂z/∂w — the derivative of the weighted sum with respect to the weight = the input xᵢ

Each layer only needs the gradient flowing from the layer above — this is why it's called backpropagation: gradients flow backward through the network, layer by layer.

Gradient Descent — Updating the Weights

Once you have ∂L/∂w for every weight, you update each weight to reduce the loss:

w_new = w_old - η × ∂L/∂w

# η (eta) = learning rate — how big a step to take
# ∂L/∂w = gradient — which direction increases loss (we go opposite)

# Too large η: overshoot the minimum → training diverges
# Too small η: very slow convergence, may get stuck
Optimiser How it works Use when
SGD Fixed learning rate; update after each mini-batch Computer vision with momentum; when you want full control
Adam ✅ Adapts learning rate per weight; momentum + RMS scaling Default for most tasks — almost always works well
AdamW Adam + proper weight decay (L2 regularisation) Transformers, LLMs — best for large modern architectures

The Complete Training Loop

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

# ── Define the network ─────────────────────────────────────────
class MLP(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(4, 16),   # 4 inputs → 16 hidden neurons
            nn.ReLU(),          # activation
            nn.Linear(16, 8),   # 16 → 8 hidden neurons
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Dropout(0.3),    # 30% dropout for regularisation
            nn.Linear(8, 3),    # 8 → 3 output classes
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.net(x)     # Softmax applied by the loss function

model = MLP()
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=0.001)
loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()  # includes softmax

# ── Training loop ──────────────────────────────────────────────
for epoch in range(100):
    model.train()
    for X_batch, y_batch in dataloader:    # mini-batches of 32
        optimizer.zero_grad()              # clear previous gradients
        predictions = model(X_batch)       # forward pass → ŷ
        loss = loss_fn(predictions, y_batch)  # measure error
        loss.backward()                    # backprop → ∂L/∂w for all w
        optimizer.step()                   # w ← w − η·∂L/∂w

    # ── Validation ────────────────────────────────────────────
    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():                  # no gradients needed for eval
        val_preds = model(X_val)
        val_loss = loss_fn(val_preds, y_val)
    print(f"Epoch {epoch}: train={loss:.4f}  val={val_loss:.4f}")

Overfitting and Regularisation

A deep network with millions of weights can memorise the training data — achieving 99% training accuracy but 60% on new data. This is overfitting.

How to detect overfitting

Plot training loss vs validation loss over epochs. If training loss keeps falling but validation loss starts rising → overfitting. The gap between them is the generalisation error.

Dropout

Randomly zero out 20–50% of neurons during each training forward pass. Forces the network to learn redundant representations — no single neuron can be relied upon. At test time, all neurons are active but scaled.

L2 Regularisation (Weight Decay)

Adds a penalty λ·||w||² to the loss. Keeps all weights small — prevents any single weight from dominating. Equivalent to placing a Gaussian prior on weights. Use AdamW for this in practice.

Batch Normalisation

Normalises activations within each mini-batch so they have mean≈0, std≈1. Stabilises training, allows higher learning rates, and has a mild regularising effect. Inserted between linear and activation layers.

Early Stopping

Monitor validation loss. Stop training when it stops improving for N consecutive epochs. Save the weights from the best validation epoch. Simple and highly effective — the most common regularisation in practice.

The Vanishing Gradient Problem

Deep networks trained with sigmoid/tanh activations hit a critical failure: gradients shrink exponentially as they travel backwards through many layers.

The sigmoid derivative is at most 0.25. Backpropagating through 10 layers:

0.25¹⁰ = 0.0000001 ≈ 0 → early layers receive almost zero gradient signal → stop learning

What solved it (and made deep learning possible):

  • ReLU activation — gradient = 1 for z > 0. No shrinkage.
  • Batch Normalisation — keeps activations in a healthy range throughout training
  • Residual connections (ResNets) — direct "skip" paths allow gradients to flow back without passing through every layer
  • Better weight initialisation — He init for ReLU, Glorot/Xavier for tanh/sigmoid

Key Concepts Summary

Concept What it means Key number / detail
Weight How strongly an input influences a neuron's output Learned via gradient descent
Bias Constant offset; shifts the activation threshold One per neuron; learned like weights
Forward pass Input → Z[l] = Wa + b → A[l] = f(Z) → prediction Layer by layer, left to right
Loss How wrong the prediction is; what we minimise MSE / Cross-Entropy
Backpropagation Chain rule applied backwards → ∂L/∂w for every weight Right to left through all layers
Gradient descent w ← w − η·∂L/∂w — step weights downhill on loss surface η = learning rate (e.g. 0.001)
Epoch One full pass through the entire training dataset Typically 10–1000 epochs
Dropout Randomly zero neurons during training; prevents overfitting Typically 20–50% drop rate
